table.text: Given the large size of the Scopus dataset, all analyses were expected to achieve the required 95% power. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

text.text: Scientific collaboration, often measured through co-authorship, has grown in many disciplines and is frequently linked to increased citation rates.
However, it remains unclear which disciplines have seen the greatest growth in collaboration and how this growth relates to article-level metrics.
Moreover, little is known about how team demographics (e.g., h-index, gender, number of institutions) and team size interact with regard to research impact.
Understanding these dynamics is essential given their influence on hiring, tenure, and the broader scientific ecosystem.
Using metadata from Elsevier's International Center for the Study of Research (ICSR) Lab, we examined collaboration trends across disciplines and their associations with citation outcomes.

The number of co-authors on a project (i.e., team size, proxied here by the length of the authorship list) has been increasing in many fields of study, such as biomedical sciences (Papatheodorou et al., 2008), medicine (Weeks et al., 2004), and psychology (Zafrunnisha & Reddy, 2010).

text.text: Notably, the number of co-authors is one factor that may be positively associated with article metrics (e.g., citation rates, Larivière et al., 2015; Wuchty et al., 2007), although the extent of this relationship may vary by field (e.g., physics, Hinnant et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Notably, the number of co-authors is one factor that may be positively associated with article metrics (e.g., citation rates, <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Larivière et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">Wuchty et al., 2007)</ref>, although the extent of this relationship may vary by field (e.g., physics, <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Hinnant et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Within coauthored papers, additional characteristics of the authorship team may be related to these metrics.

Author diversity, broadly speaking, has been associated with positive outcomes such as publication in high-impact factor journals, rates of citations, and funding (Freeman & Huang, 2015; Nichols, 2014).

text.text: It is important to note that author diversity can be conceptualized along a continuum of factors such as gender, physical location (e.g., United States, Brazil), institutional affiliation, discipline, and rank.

Evidence suggests the impact of international collaboration, rank, and gender on article metrics in fields such as sport science research (Wang et al., 2015), physics (Hinnant et al., 2012), and psychology (Geraci et al., 2015), respectively.

text.text: Despite the benefits of having diversity among co-authors for scientific productivity and impact, co-author teams tend to be homogenous (e.g., within a cancer research center, Fagan et al., 2018).

text.text: For example, when looking at gender, authors exhibit a tendency to work with others of the same gender, a finding that is consistent over time (Whittington et al., 2023).

text.text: Thus, recommendations for scientists to diversify or broaden their co-author networks may not be effective without careful consideration of team size and composition.

Consistent with this, simply enlarging a collaboration team or seeking well-connected collaborators is not always the best strategy for research performance, and the best approach depends on a scholar's own research variety and goals (Zhu et al., 2021).

text.text: The available research paints an incomplete picture of co-authorship trends and their relationship to citation metrics.

Landmark studies have documented the growth of team size and its association with citations over long time spans (e.g., 1900 spans (e.g., -2011 spans (e.g., , Larivière et al., 2015;; 1955 -2000 , Wuchty et al., 2007)), and the gender gap in authorship has been studied across countries, disciplines, and career stages (Huang et al., 2020; Larivière et al., 2013).

text.text: However, these literatures have largely developed separately, and less is known about how team size and several features of team composition (gender, the h-index of the first and last authors, and the number of institutions and countries represented) are jointly related to article-level citation metrics within and across disciplines in a single, contemporary, article-level dataset.
Understanding co-author team composition is therefore critical, given previous research showing that, despite the benefits of co-authorship diversity, people tend to work with those similar to them.

As such, this project aims to first establish trends in co-authorship team size within disciplines across time and then explore how the composition of these co-authorship teams is related to citation metrics.
The research questions guiding these aims are as follows: 1a.)
What is the pattern of team size distribution within various disciplines over time, 1b.) is team size related to article impact?, and 2.)
What characteristics of team composition have the strongest association with article metrics?
Question 1.
What is the pattern of team size distribution within various disciplines over time, and is team size related to article impact?

Initiatives, calls, and funding opportunities for collaborative research (from both private and public/government sectors) have been increasing in recent years, with some arguing that large teams (i.e., co-authors) are necessary for addressing modern societal questions and problems (Samarasekera, 2009).

text.text: Discipline-specific investigations have identified co-authorship trends that differ by subdiscipline.

For example, over approximately 30 years the average number of authors roughly doubled in four major musculoskeletal science journals (from 3.67 to 7.3 authors per article) (Russell et al., 2019), whereas team sizes in mathematics have remained small, rising from an average of 1.10 authors per paper in the 1940s to 1.63 in the 1990s (Grossman, 2002).

text.text: Among the social sciences, a more consistent pattern of increased co-authorship emerged, although specific changes vary by subfield (De Meuse et al., 2014; Gaunt, 2014; Hunter & Leahey, 2008; Kozlowski et al., 2017; Rath & Wohlrabe, 2016).

text.text: This suggests that needs and norms within various disciplines may influence how quickly and to what extent authorship trends change and solidify.

Because the current state of the research focuses on constructs like time period (e.g., eleven years of one journal, Abu and Verma (2019)), a single publication such as one handbook (De Meuse et al., 2014), and geographical region (Leifeld et al., 2017) in isolation, examining co-authorship trends among multiple disciplines concurrently would afford a more holistic overview of the state of team science.

text.text: The CEM provides a conceptual rationale for examining the present variables together.

Gender is a social-category characteristic of the team; the number of institutions and countries represented index affiliation-based (and likely information-based) diversity; and the h-index of the first and last authors indexes the status and expertise that authors bring to the team.

Team size sets the number of people among whom these differences can be distributed, and is therefore both a covariate for and a context of the composition variables (indeed, institution and country counts cannot exceed team size).

We selected these variables because they are the author-level characteristics available at scale in the Scopus metadata, and we treat them as correlates of citation metrics rather than as causal mechanisms.
This research on team diversity must also be considered alongside sociocultural research about how members of certain groups have historically been treated in the sciences.

text.text: One commonly used measure of a scholar's output and impact is the "h-index" (Hirsch, 2005).

text.text: The h-index combines the number of articles published with the number of citations received for those articles.
This approach attempts to balance high-impact articles with the number of articles published.
Specifically, the h-score is the number of articles (X) that receive X citations.

The h-index is one of the most widely used measures of a scholar's impact (Crespo & Simoes, 2019), although it has also been criticized, for example for its dependence on field and career length and for behaving inconsistently when comparing scholars (Bornmann & Daniel, 2007; Waltman & van Eck, 2012).

text.text: All variables extracted from this dataset are described below.
Article characteristics included the year of publication, number of authors (team size), and discipline.

Team size was operationalized as the number of authors on the article's authorship list; this is a common proxy for the size of the team that produced the work, but it is not strictly synonymous with it (e.g., it excludes acknowledged contributors).

Discipline was defined using the All Science Journal Classification (ASJC; https://service.elsevier.com/app/answers/detail/a_id/15181/supporthub/scopus/) with the five global subject area codes (Health, Physical, Life, Social Sciences, and Multidisciplinary).

Articles whose journals fell outside the four named areas were classified as Multidisciplinary.

Metric characteristics included citation count (the number of times an article was cited within the current data snapshot, including self-citations) and five-year citation count (the number of citations received within five years of publication, as supplied in the ICSR fieldweighted citation impact table; this is the raw count, not the field-normalized ratio).

Author characteristics included affiliation country, affiliation/institution, h-index, gender, and gender ratio.
We transformed affiliation countries into a count variable of the number of unique countries.
Similarly, we transformed affiliation/institutions into a count of the number of different affiliations across authors.
We used the h-index of the first and last authors for each article, with and without self-citation.
Author position was used as recorded; we did not assume that the last author is the most senior member of the team (see Limitations).
Last, Elsevier has noted that their inferred gender column has a 97% accuracy, and we used the inferred gender of the first and last authors for each article.
From this variable, we additionally calculated the gender ratio (number of inferred male / total authors) as a single variable for each article.
While Scopus includes articles from 1788 to present, we limited our sample to journal articles published from 1970 until the date of the data snapshot.
Scopus indicates that articles from 1970 to present include reference information, which was required to calculate several of the above mentioned variables.
We originally planned to include all eligible articles from 1970 forward.
Due to computational constraints, we randomly sampled 25% of eligible articles during this time span to constrain the run time of our code and the memory necessary to calculate h-index.

Articles were sampled by simple random sampling (fixed seed), so the sample is expected to be representative of the eligible population, and with several million articles per subject area the sampling error is negligible.
However, we did not compare the sample with the full population, nor repeat the sampling, so we cannot demonstrate representativeness across publication years or subject areas; this is a limitation.
It is important to note that we did not calculate h-index on the randomly sampled dataset.
These values were calculated on the full data and then merged with the randomly sampled data to ensure h-indices were appropriate for authors on the randomly sampled data.

Nearly all scatter plots indicated heteroscedasticity, and team size and citation counts are discrete, non-negative, and highly right-skewed (with many uncited articles), which are conditions under which count models (e.g., Poisson or negative binomial, possibly zero-inflated) are often preferred.

We retained ordinary least squares linear models for three reasons: (a) they were specified in our preregistration; (b) with samples of this size, inference about the slopes does not depend on the normality of the residuals; and (c) the slopes are directly interpretable as the expected difference in citations per additional author (or per one-unit difference in an author characteristic), which we use throughout.

However, the standard errors and confidence intervals from these models should be interpreted cautiously given the heteroscedasticity, and the linear models may misrepresent the conditional mean at the extremes of the distribution.
We did not run negative binomial, zeroinflated, or other count-data models, and we no longer have access to the data to do so; this is a limitation of the present work.

Discussion Question 1.
What is the pattern of team size distribution within various disciplines over time, and is team size related to article impact?
The first research question in this paper addressed the pattern of team size distribution within various disciplines over time and the relationship between team size and article impact.

Our findings indicate a consistent increase in team size across disciplines, corroborating previous research on the expansion of scientific collaboration (Larivière et al., 2015; Wuchty et al., 2007).

text.text: The trend was most pronounced in the physical sciences.

This is consistent with reports of substantial rises in team size in other natural science fields, such as musculoskeletal science (Russell et al., 2019) and biology (Nabout et al., 2015), over the past few decades, although those studies did not examine physics.

Looking at authorship and acknowledgment trends concurrently may represent an important area of future research that illuminates authorship norms among various disciplines and guides conversations about crediting.

Despite this variation, the broader increase in co-authorship aligns with the necessity of interdisciplinary and large-scale collaborations to address complex scientific challenges (Samarasekera, 2009).

text.text: These trends may be influenced by funding opportunities favoring collaborative efforts, the need for diverse expertise in tackling intricate research questions, and the growing complexity of modern scientific inquiry.

Our analysis also found a positive association between team size and article impact, as measured by citation counts, consistent with previous findings that collaborative works tend to garner more citations (Thijs et al., 2015; Wuchty et al., 2007).

text.text: These data are observational, and the association should not be read as team size driving citations.

It may partly reflect characteristics that co-occur with larger teams, such as disciplines in which both team size and citation counts are high; our by-discipline analyses show that the association was present within each of the five broad subject areas, but these areas remain coarse (e.g., large-team fields such as particle physics and genomics are grouped with smaller-team fields), so residual disciplinary differences cannot be ruled out, and finer-grained disciplinary controls could change the estimates.
One potential explanation for the association is the increased dissemination of collaborative research through multiple authors' networks, leading to broader recognition and citation.

Larger teams may also bring more collective expertise, which could improve the robustness and credibility of findings (Larivière et al., 2015), and larger teams have more opportunities for self-citation, which would inflate citation counts because our citation outcomes included self-citations.

While the relationship between team size and citations appears generally positive, it is not necessarily linear.

Prior studies have suggested that citation benefits plateau beyond a certain threshold (e.g., approximately 20 authors), indicating diminishing returns for excessively large teams (Sharma, 2021; Zhu et al., 2021).

Future research should explore potential moderators, such as discipline-specific authorship norms and the role of team leadership in fostering impactful collaborations.
Gender composition was associated with citation rates, though the associations varied by discipline.
We caution against interpreting these patterns as an effect of author gender on citing behavior.
Readers frequently cannot infer authors' gender (e.g., from initials or unfamiliar names), and researchers generally cite work for its relevance, novelty, methodological quality, or venue.

A more plausible reading is that gender is correlated with other factors that we did not model, such as career stage, institutional prestige, funding, journal quality, topic, and finer-grained disciplinary differences, as well as with disciplinary norms regarding authorship position, scientific networks, and systemic inequities in academia.

Consistent with prior research, our results indicate that male-dominated authorship teams tended to receive fewer citations in social sciences and health sciences, whereas in some disciplines, particularly the life sciences, male first authors were associated with higher citation counts (Maliniak et al., 2013; West et al., 2013).

Future research should explore how variations in h-index across disciplines and career stages affect long-term scholarly impact.
The limitations of h-index as a universal metric must also be acknowledged.
It does not account for field-specific citation norms, and early-career researchers and those publishing in niche areas may be at a disadvantage.

In addition, we used the h-index of the last author as an indicator of an experienced author, but authorship conventions differ across disciplines (e.g., alphabetical ordering or other author-order practices), so the last author is not necessarily the most senior member of the team, and the first/last author comparison may be biased in fields that do not follow the first/last convention.
Alternative bibliometric indicators, such as the i10-index or g-index, may provide complementary insights into scholarly impact by addressing some of these limitations.
Moreover, as open-access publishing continues to rise, its potential impact on citation disparities linked to h-index should be explored further.
In summary, our study documents the growing prominence of scientific collaboration and its association with citation metrics.

Team size and institutional and international diversity were positively associated with citation counts, and gender representation also showed varied associations with citations that differed by discipline.
These associations were small in magnitude: the models explained, at most, about 7% of the variance in citations, and the author variables explained only a fraction of that.
Statistical significance was assured by the size of the dataset, so the practical size of the effects is what matters for interpretation.
Limitations.
The analyses are observational, so the associations cannot be interpreted causally.

We used linear models for count outcomes that are skewed and heteroscedastic; used five broad subject areas that hide large differences in collaboration practices within them; did not control for journal quality, career stage, institutional prestige, or funding; and included self-citations in the citation outcomes.
The h-index is a contested measure, and last-author position is an imperfect proxy for seniority.
Gender was inferred rather than self-reported, and we analyzed a 25% random sample of eligible articles.

Because we no longer have access to the ICSR data, we could not present the distributions of team size and citations beyond summary statistics and capped boxplots, report descriptive statistics for the author variables, or run additional models.
Any of these may account for part of the observed associations.
Implications.

Given the small effect sizes and the likelihood of confounding, these findings do not support using team size, team composition, or author h-index as stand-alone indicators in research evaluation, funding allocation, hiring, or promotion decisions; such uses risk rewarding correlates of citation counts rather than the quality or contribution of the work.

They are better suited to describing how collaboration practices differ across fields and to informing institutional policies that remove barriers to inclusive collaboration (for example, by supporting cross-institution and international partnerships and by examining how credit is assigned in teams) without presuming that such collaboration will in itself raise citation counts.

Future research should test these relationships with models suited to count data (e.g., negative binomial), include interactions among team size, time, and composition variables, add journal-level and career-stage controls, and use finer-grained subject classifications.

Additionally, exploring the intersectionality of gender, institutional affiliation, and career stage could provide a more nuanced understanding of how different factors are jointly related to research visibility and impact.

Finally, the recent adoption of large language models (LLMs) in research and writing may be changing how researchers collaborate and how teams are formed, for example by changing the amount of work that can be done by small teams or by lowering barriers across languages and disciplines.

Whether team sizes and collaboration patterns have shifted since the widespread availability of LLMs is an empirical question that our data, which end at the data snapshot date, were not designed to address; the trends reported here provide a pre-LLM baseline against which such changes could be evaluated in future team science research.
As the scientific enterprise continues to evolve, ensuring equitable and inclusive collaboration practices will be essential.

The authors made the following contributions.
Kelly Cuccolo:
You can find these results by going to 01_prereg and opening team_science_analysis.html.
We ran these analyses on our first pilot code.
They are more detailed than the second analysis code (i.e., we could pinpoint specific subareas within the final five areas analyzed), so we used the smaller analyses for data screening.
The results are summarized here.
By searching for stat.corr within the code, you can find the correlations with there are multiple independent variables within a regression analysis.
They are usually printed at the bottom of a scatter plot.
The correlations for research question 1 were all very low rs from .02 to .30.
The correlations for research question 2 were similarly low with two exceptions: r ~ .50-.53 for team size and number of countries and r ~ .71-74 for team size and institution count.
Given the number of countries and institutions can only be as high as the number of authors, these values are not surprising.
Further, they did not meet our exclusion criteria of r > .90 overall.

text.text: Institution count for Earth Sciences correlated with team size at r ~ .902-.908 but no other values were found.
Given the more generalized subject areas, the average r for these two variables was considered ok for use for the category that includes Earth Sciences.
